extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of American political history (late 19th-century California), general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close, narrative analysis of the rise, actions, and consequences of the Kearney/Sand Lot movement and the 1879 California Constitution, with attention to causes, constitutional provisions, political dynamics, and lessons. Suitable for historical/political- science study of populist movements and constitutional reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the Granger/Sand Lot movement
rubrics_metrics.description: To compel a reduction of charges for goods and passengers; to prevent the railroad from combining with the Panama Steamship Company; to reduce public expenditure; to shift more taxation on to the shoulders of the rich; and generally to 'cinch' capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aims were seen as partly reasonable in California; the text argues the only effective route to achieve them was a new Constitution because a convention gives more direct control to the people than a legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for using a constitutional convention
rubrics_metrics.description: A convention is preferred because delegates 'go straight from the election to their work', have less time to forget or evade pledges, are less liable to be 'got at' by capitalists, constitute only one house (no governor veto), and the rarity/importance of the occasion fixes public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why the movement sought structural constitutional change rather than legislative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and competence of convention delegates
rubrics_metrics.description: Workingmen's Party (W.P.C.) nominees were mostly ignorant men without experience or constructive ideas; lawyers formed a large representation, some bound to corporate interests and others seeking to restrain folly by respect for common law and constitutional doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination of inexperienced W.P.C. delegates and corporate-tied lawyers produced an instrument (the 1879 Constitution) surprising in its content; anecdotes of delegates' ignorance illustrate limits of competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four principal grievances the Constitution aimed to address
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) The general corruption of politicians and bad conduct of State, county, and city government; 2) Taxation, alleged to press too heavily on the poorer classes; 3) The tyranny of corporations, especially railroads; 4) The Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames subsequent constitutional provisions as responses to these four problems and then evaluates their effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional restriction on legislative power and criminalization of lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: It restricts and limits in every possible way the powers of the State legislature, leaving it little authority except to carry out the Constitution; it makes 'lobbying', i.e. the attempt to corrupt a legislator, and the corrupt action of a legislator, felony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as part of the Convention's contributions toward 'None but honest men for the offices.' The text later notes that corporate influence persisted despite these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal and taxation measures in the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: It forbids the State legislature or local authorities to incur debts beyond a certain limit; taxes uncultivated land equally with cultivated; makes sums due on mortgage taxable where the mortgaged property lies; authorizes an income tax; and directs a highly inquisitorial scrutiny of everybody's property for taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions aim to curb public expenditure and shift taxation, but are evaluated in context of their economic and political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate-regulatory provisions and railroad oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: It forbids 'watering of stock', declares State power to prevent corporations from conducting business so as to 'infringe the general well-being of the State', directs telegraph/gas/water charges to be regulated and limited by law, institutes a railroad commission with power to fix transportation rates and examine books and accounts of transportation companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to curb perceived corporate tyranny; later sections evaluate implementation problems (capture of commissions, lack of practical knowledge among commissioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Chinese constitutional provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: It forbids all corporations to employ any Chinese; debars them from the suffrage; forbids their employment on any public works; annuls all contracts for 'coolie labour'; directs the legislature to punish companies importing Chinese; to impose conditions on Chinese residence and provide for their removal if conditions are not observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes this attempts to 'transgress the fifteenth amendment' and places the anti-Chinese measures among the Constitution's most controversial elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight-hour workday on public works
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution declares that eight hours shall constitute a legal day's work on all public works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This labor-protective clause is listed among the instrument's provisions addressing working-class grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal constitutional check and judicial invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some provisions were alleged to be opposed to the Constitution of the United States and therefore null; several statutes framed under the 1879 Constitution were pronounced invalid by the State Supreme Court as opposed to that instrument or the Federal Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal constitution serves as a corrective check on state-level radical provisions; courts subsequently pruned and checked the 1879 instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-ratification political dynamics and corporate influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Constitution was submitted and carried, conservative elements and corporate money influenced subsequent legislative elections and statute implementation; Republicans often adhered to the letter of the Constitution while workingmen/farmers sought to follow its 'spirit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how institutional politics and money worked to blunt radical measures despite constitutional language criminalizing lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and ineffectiveness of regulatory bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: When the railroad commission had to be elected, railroad magnates influenced the election so that two of the three commissioners chosen were, or soon came, under their influence and the third was a mere declaimer; none possessed practical knowledge needed to deal with railway oppressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit anti-capture lesson: formal regulatory powers can be hollow if oversight bodies are captured or lack expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of the movement's rapid rise
rubrics_metrics.description: It rose with surprising ease and swiftness due to exceptionally favourable conditions: hard times, a demagogic leader who rode the crest of a wave, regional demographics, and alliances (e.g., with the Granger movement and farmers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses both structural conditions and contingent leadership shortcomings as explanatory factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of the movement's decline
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement fell quickly due to the incompetence of its leader (Kearney), absence of constructive proposals, the strength of the existing American party system which makes creating a new permanent party difficult, and the withdrawal of moderate support once initial goals appeared achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains durability dynamics of local populist movements and the protective effect of established party structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of 'respectable' classes and law enforcement in checking disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: The police and militia behaved well and small hoodlums who attacked Chinese stores disappeared at the sight of police; respectable classes would supersede municipal authority if it feared or conspired with sedition; meetings were seldom seriously disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers an argument that social order, backed by respectable citizens, constrains the potential for mob anarchy in American cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the movement: not communistic; entrenchment of vested rights
rubrics_metrics.description: There was very little conscious or constructive communism or socialism; the new Constitution 'entrenches vested rights, especially in land, more thoroughly than before', levies a poll tax without exemption, disfranchises a portion of floating labour, and in various ways sacrifices labouring classes to landowners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text refutes Eastern claims of communistic character and argues the instrument actually protected certain vested interests while harming others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net practical consequences of the agitation and Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The net result was to give monied classes a fright, win the State a bad name, check the influx of capital and retard growth, worry corporations without seriously crippling them, and leave working classes and farmers largely where they were; courts pruned the document and amendments often made it more 'radical'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates outcomes: limited harm but also limited benefit; political reputational and economic side-effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salient features / lessons about perversions of popular government
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of an organization in a multitude; the facility with which administrative machinery may be made the instrument of private gain; and the disposition of the average respectable citizen to submit to bad government rather than take the trouble of overthrowing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized moral drawn from the California and Ring examples; intended as cautionary lessons about democratic vulnerability and administrative corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for party durability: central and local organization
rubrics_metrics.description: A new party cannot count itself permanent until it has established some central as well as local organization; existing parties are strong and hard to displace because of complex local organizations supported by central organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains organizational preconditions for converting ephemeral movements into lasting political forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlook on future shocks and the strength of order
rubrics_metrics.description: Although socialistic doctrines might make future shocks more violent than that of 1879, such shocks are likely to remain within legal limits; there seems no danger of mere mob law and anarchy because 'the forces at the disposal of order are always the stronger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A predictive normative judgment about stability: legal/institutional order and social forces will tend to contain future disturbances.
